summary: An excerpt from a fiction passage (labeled Book 15, part 78) in which Ray and Emma flirt closely, with Emma remarking on his loneliness and calling him lonely for her. Ray, distracted, reflects on loneliness as a step toward desperation and recalls how, as a military leader, he sent his soldiers to get release before battles because it steadied them emotionally. He then rejects her claim that he is lonely, and the passage ends with Emma's concern at his distraction and his admission that he has never said anything like that to a woman.
one_line: Ray and Emma flirt intimately while Ray, distracted, reflects on loneliness and on the pre-battle release he once arranged for his soldiers.
key_facts: Ray tells Emma she is the most beautiful thing he has ever seen, and says that his feelings for her scare him.
Emma tells Ray that he has been lonely for a very long time.
Ray asks Emma whether she would have come that night if she were not lonely, and she has no direct answer in the excerpt.
Ray reflects that loneliness is a step away from desperation and that lonely men make stupid mistakes.
Ray recalls that before a major tactical engagement he made his men go into the nearest town for sex or release, and that he gave money to any soldier who could not afford it.
Ray believes the pre-battle release left soldiers with brighter eyes, firmer steps and less trembling hands, though they remained scared.
Ray thinks getting laid would not save soldiers' lives on the battlefield, but it gave them a perspective that kept them from making fatal mistakes.
Ray tells Emma that he is not lonely, and Emma replies that he is lonely for her and lonely and hungry.
Ray wonders what mistakes he might be making or essential facts he might be missing if his loneliness is obvious to someone he has just met.
Emma's voice shifts from playful to questioning and concerned because Ray has drifted into his own thoughts instead of answering her flirtation.
Ray says he has never said anything like that to a woman, and Emma responds with delight, asking 'Never?'
